power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Personalized information environments have been proposed to contribute to political polarization, yet empirical findings remain mixed.
The present work aimed to clarify these inconsistencies by distinguishing between different polarization outcomes and considering individual characteristics as potential moderators.

In an online experiment, we tested how attitude-congruency of information environments affects issue and affective polarization regarding unconditional basic income (UBI) in Germany, and whether Intellectual Humility (IH) and Need for Cognitive Closure (NfCC) moderate these effects.
N = 756 participants were exposed to one of three information environments containing predominantly attitudecongruent, attitude-incongruent, or neutral statements about UBI.

Affective polarization was assessed separately as the divide in negative affective evaluations (stronger negative feelings toward the outgroup than ingroup; NAD) and the divide in positive affective evaluations (PAD; stronger positive feelings toward the ingroup than outgroup) between issue-based groups.
Compared with neutral exposure, attitude-congruent information increased issue polarization, NAD, and PAD.
Attitude-incongruent information decreased issue polarization but had no signficant effect on either affective divide.
IH was positively associated with and moderated effects on PAD.
NfCC showed no effects.

Findings highlight the importance of distinguishing between polarization outcomes and suggest that positive and negative affective intergroup divides may show different associations with individual characteristics.

Rising political polarization is a concern in many societies including countries in the European Union: Perceptions of a broken society (Ipsos, 2025) and an increasing divide in opinions (Wissenschaft im Dialog gGmbH, 2025) are widespread in public opinion according to recent surveys.

Against the background of the aforementioned literature and conceptual considerations, the present study aims to establish a clearer link between attitude-congruent and attitude-incongruent information environments and both issue and affective polarization, where we divide affective polarization into a positive and a negative affective facet.

To do so, we compare information environments containing attitude-congruent statements, attitudeincongruent statements, or neutral statements about a political issue: the introduction of an unconditional basic income (UBI) in Germany.

Considering that both theoretical accounts (Pariser, 2012) and a majority of empirical evidence seems to suggest a positive link between attitude-congruent information environments and political polarization (Kubin & Von Sikorski, 2021), we hypothesize the following for the impact of attitude-congruent information: H1: Exposure to attitude-congruent information increases issue polarization (H1a) and affective polarization, reflected in higher negative affect toward the issue-based political outgroup relative to the ingroup (NAD; H1b) and higher positive affect toward the political ingroup compared to the outgroup (PAD; H1c). or depolarizes or has no effect.

NfCC refers to the tendency to seek definite conclusions or answers (closure) and avoid or minimize ambiguity and uncertainty (Roets & Van Hiel, 2011).

text.text: It is characterized by a tendency to quickly find closure (urgency tendency), and a tendency to preserve and safeguard closure (permanence tendency), also referred to as "seize" and "freeze" (Kruglanski & Webster, 1996).

text.text: In line with this account, high NfCC has been linked to reduced consideration of alternatives, greater confidence in judgment, intolerance for dissenting views, stronger intergroup bias, including ingroup favoritism and outgroup animosity (Kruglanski et al., 2010; Luttig, 2018; Mayseless & Kruglanski, 1987; Shah et al., 1998; Webster & Kruglanski, 1997).

After providing demographic information, participants reported their political orientation and completed an attention-check item.
Next, they read an explanation of the UBI which specified parameters for the policy as understood in the context of the present study.
Afterward, participants answered two additional attentioncheck items assessing comprehension of the UBI description.
Participants subsequently reported their baseline attitudes toward the UBI as well as their positive and negative feelings toward supporters and opponents of the UBI, respectively.
They were then randomly assigned to one of three information environments, each containing 30 statements.
The statements were mostly either in favor of, against, or neutral toward the UBI, depending on the experimental condition.
Afterwards, participants again reported their attitudes toward the UBI and their feelings toward UBI supporters and opponents.
They then completed questionnaires assessing intellectual humility and NfCC.
Finally, participants estimated the percentage of the population in Germany that shares their attitude toward the UBI and reported the personal relevance of the UBI to them.
Participants were exposed to one of three information environments.
In the "pro UBI" environment, participants were presented with 24 statements in favor of the UBI and six neutral statements.
In the "contra UBI" information environment, participants saw 24 statements against the UBI and the six neutral statements.
Finally, in the neutral information environment, participants were exposed to 30 neutral statements, including the same six neutral statements as for the two other environments.
Assignment to the three information environments was randomized, with quotas ensuring a comparable distribution of UBI supporters and opponents across information environments.

The valenced statements were selected from a pool of pre-tested UBI statements so that, based on pre-test data, the set of statements in favor of the UBI and the set of statements against the UBI did not differ significantly in terms of absolute valence, importance, plausibility, familiarity, and comprehensibility ratings, as well as reading time.
Further information on the creation of the pool of statements as well as the selection method can be taken from the Supplementary Materials.
The neutral set of statements was taken from Jalbert et al.'s (2019) trivia claim statement pool and translated into German.

text.text: All statements had a length between nine and 14 words.
Participants' attitudes toward the UBI were assessed at baseline as well as after the experimental manipulation using a 4-item scale.

The scale contained three items that measure attitudes toward the expected impact of the UBI on the economy, culture and life quality, as well as one item assessing overall support/opposition for the UBI.
Participants responded to each item on an 11-point scale ranging from 0 (indicating a very negative evaluation) to 10 (indicating a very positive evaluation).
Consistent with previous findings (study currently under review), the UBI scale showed an internal consistency estimate of Cronbach's ⍺ = .92 in the present sample.
Details on the development and validation of the UBI scale can be taken from the Supplementary Materials.

The measure of (state) issue polarization was then calculated separately for preexperiment (baseline measure) and post-experiment assessments as the absolute distance of the aggregated UBI attitude score from the theoretical midpoint of the scale (5.00).

Participants were classified as UBI supporters or UBI opponents based on their baseline UBI attitude score: scores above 5.00 indicated supporters and scores below 5.00 indicated opponents (participants scoring exactly 5 were excluded; see exclusion criteria).

For each participant, the issue-based ingroup was defined as the attitude group matching their own stance (supporters rating supporters; opponents rating opponents), and the issue-based outgroup as the opposing stance (supporters rating opponents; opponents rating supporters).

Before and after the experimental manipulation, participants reported their negative feelings towards supporters and opponents of the UBI on 101-point scales ranging from 0 ("Gar nicht negativ"; not negative at all) to 100 ("Sehr negativ"; very negative), rating supporters and opponents separately.
The CIHS scale showed an internal consistency estimate of Cronbach's ⍺ = .89.
Participants' need for cognitive closure (NfCC) was assessed using the German short scale developed by Schlink and Walther (2007).

The present study examined whether experimentally constructed attitude-congruent and attitude-incongruent information environments shape political polarization in the context of attitudes toward the introduction of a UBI.
More specifically, it investigated effects on issue polarization as well as on the negative and positive evaluative components of affective polarization, separately.
In addition, it examined whether these effects are moderated by intellectual humility and NfCC.
Our results revealed four main findings.
First, exposure to attitude-congruent information increased issue polarization as well as the negative and positive affective divides in intergroup evaluations.

Thus, the findings largely support the expectation that information environments dominated by information congruent with an individual's pre-existing attitudes can foster political polarization (hypothesis H1a-c).

This pattern is in line with theoretical accounts (Levendusky, 2013a; Pariser, 2012; Sunstein, 2007) and empirical work (Kelm et al., 2023; Kubin & von Sikorski, 2021; Levendusky, 2013a; Ludwig et al., 2023) linking personalized information environments to political polarization.

text.text: Regarding RQ1, the effect of attitude-congruent information was descriptively largest for issue polarization, followed by PAD and smallest on NAD.
Second, our results indicate a depolarizing effect of attitude-incongruent information on issue polarization.
However, they provide no evidence of such an effect on either affective polarization measure.
Although the estimated effects on NAD and PAD were negative, they did not reach statistical significance.

Therefore, our findings are consistent with accounts suggesting that exposure to cross-cutting content can reduce polarization (Barberá, 2015) but provide no evidence of the backlash effects suggested by accounts of motivated cognition (Levendusky, 2013b).

text.text: These results should, however, be qualified insofar as the information environment to which participants were exposed to did not contain any attitude-congruent information.
This limits comparability with interventions that present more balanced media diets or increase attitude-incongruent information without excluding congruent information entirely.
It is possible that whether attitude-incongruent information leads to depolarization or backlash depends on the ratio between attitude-congruent and -incongruent information.

For instance, responses to incongruent information may shift from defensive processing toward attitude revision after tipping point is reached and accuracy motivations take over (Redlawsk et al., 2010).

text.text: Nonetheless, the effect of exclusively attitude-incongruent information provides an informative benchmark test.
Third, regarding moderators, our results suggest an association between intellectual humility and PAD.
However, this relationship is not straightforward.

On the one hand, higher intellectual humility was related to higher PAD in the neutral information environment, contrasting with previous findings that suggest a negative relationship between intellectual humility and affective polarization (Knöchelmann & Cohrs, 2024).

text.text: On the other hand, the polarizing effect of attitude-congruent information on PAD was attenuated for individuals higher in intellectual humility, in line with its proposed buffering effect (Bowes et al., 2020).

text.text: However, considering that the inclusion of the interaction terms did not significantly improve overall model fit and that conclusions regarding both the main effect of intellectual humility on PAD and its interaction with the congruent information environment were sensitive to the type of SEs used in the analyses, these findings should be interpreted with caution.
Further evidence is needed to more conclusively determine the role of intellectual humility in the context of congruent information exposure.
Regarding NfCC, we found no evidence of an association with any polarization outcome, nor evidence that NfCC moderated the effects of attitude-congruent or attitude-incongruent information exposure.
Thus, the results do not support the expectation that individuals high in NfCC would be especially susceptible to reinforcement under congruent exposure or backlash under incongruent exposure.

One possible explanation is that participants may not yet have held sufficiently strong or crystallized attitudes toward the UBI. After crystallization, by contrast, high NfCC should foster "freezing", including resistance to persuasion and disconfirming information that threatens existing closure.
Under this logic, heightened polarization and backlash effects among individuals high in NfCC may be more likely for issues they have firmer beliefs on.
Fourth, the present findings illustrate the value of separating polarization facets, including the differentiation of affective polarization into positive and negative components.
In particular, the finding that intellectual humility moderated the effect of attitude-congruent exposure on PAD, whereas no corresponding moderation effect was observed for NAD.
Had affective polarization been assessed only with a traditional bipolar difference score, these findings may have been harder to detect and interpret.

In line with bivariate accounts of affect such as the Evaluative Space Model (Cacioppo et al., 2012; Cacioppo & Berntson, 1994; Norris et al., 2010) and research on ambivalent attitudes (Conner & Sparks, 2002), this divergence supports the conceptual argument that positive and negative evaluations should not simply be treated as opposite poles of a single continuum.

text.text: Bipolar measures such as feeling thermometers, though convenient, may therefore obscure distinct components of group evaluation and impose an assumption of reciprocity that is conceptually contestable.

This distinction is also relevant to Röllicke's (2023) conceptualization of affective polarization, which distinguishes between increases in affective polarization (affective polarization as process) driven by growing ingroup positivity, growing outgroup negativity, or both.

text.text: Importantly, these processes need not occur simultaneously.

Accordingly, the present finding that intellectual humility moderated the effect of attitude-congruent exposure on PAD, but not NAD, suggests that positive and negative intergroup differentiation may respond differently to individual characteristics.
This study provides a controlled test of the effect of exposure to attitude-congruent and attitude-incongruent information.

Much prior work has examined polarization in platform environments in which exposure may not only be shaped by content congruence exposure alone but also by self-selection, recommendation mechanisms, and concurrent exposure to additional information (Barberá, 2020; Levy, 2021; Ludwig & Müller, 2022).

text.text: The present study cannot reproduce that ecological complexity, but it helps clarify one part of the puzzle by isolating the attitudinal congruence of exposure itself.

The finding that attitude-congruent information exposure increased all three polarization outcomes under these controlled conditions suggests that attitude congruence itself can contribute to polarization, independently of additional processes such as self-selection and platform characteristics.
A further implication of the present findings concerns the conceptualization and operationalization of affective polarization.
Affective polarization is often conceptualized in relational terms, as an evaluative gap between a political ingroup and an outgroup (Iyengar & Westwood, 2015; Röllicke, 2023; Wagner, 2021).
text.formatted: Affective polarization is often conceptualized in relational terms, as an evaluative gap between a political ingroup and an outgroup <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Iyengar & Westwood, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Röllicke, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Wagner, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, the presence of positive ingroup or negative outgroup evaluations alone does not necessarily indicate a divide in group evaluations.
For instance, individuals may hold similarly strong positive and negative evaluations of both in-and outgroups in which case no intergroup differentiation or gap would be present.

By assessing ingroup-outgroup gaps separately for positive and negative evaluations, the present operationalization preserves the relational conceptualization of affective polarization while distinguishing evaluative dimensions that are not necessarily reciprocal.
Beyond allowing for a more nuanced examination of affective polarization, this distinction has broader conceptual implications.
As Cacioppo and Berntson (1994) argue, measurement instruments shape what can be observed and how phenomena are theorized.
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cacioppo and Berntson (1994)</ref> argue, measurement instruments shape what can be observed and how phenomena are theorized.

text.text: Assessing affective polarization only with bipolar scales may therefore favor interpretations in terms of reciprocal ingroup love and outgroup hate, even when this pattern is partly imposed by the measure itself and the underlying evaluative processes are more differentiated.
This study has several limitations.

The experimental manipulation relied on constructed information environments around a single political issue, UBI, and therefore cannot speak to whether the same effects generalize across issue domains.
The design also prioritizes internal validity over ecological validity.

Real-world exposure usually involves more heterogeneous, socially embedded, and dynamically updated information streams than those presented here (Kubin & Von Sikorski, 2021; Sindermann et al., 2024; Winter et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Real-world exposure usually involves more heterogeneous, socially embedded, and dynamically updated information streams than those presented here <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Kubin & Von Sikorski, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Sindermann et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Winter et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, although the issue-based operationalization of affective polarization addresses limitations of party-based measures in multiparty settings, such measures remain less established in the literature.
Replication with other issues, populations, and measurement strategies is therefore necessary.
Further, while the separate assessment of positive and negative affective divides allows the disentanglement of both dimensions, the use of difference scores also has interpretative limitations.
Particularly, changes in these divides cannot establish whether they are driven by changes in ingroup evaluations, outgroup evaluations, or both.
Thus, although this operationalization preserves the relational conceptualization of affective polarization, it does not fully distinguish the underlying evaluative processes.

The choice between either preserving the relational aspect of affective polarization and further differentiation into singular group evaluations may depend on the question a researcher is interested in.

Overall, the present findings suggest that attitude-congruent information environments can increase both issue polarization and positive and negative affective intergroup divides, whereas attitude-incongruent environments may attenuate some but not all forms of polarization.

The findings further illustrate the value of assessing positive and negative affective components of affective polarization separately as it can reveal patterns that may have remained obscured in traditional bipolar measures of affective polarization.

Taken together, the results support a more differentiated understanding of the emergence of political polarization as a multifaceted phenomenon that depends both on the structure of the information environment and on how polarization itself is conceptualized and measured.
